# Equipment & Kits {#sec-chapter-equipment}

```{=typst}
#label("sec-chapter-equipment")

#image("assets/images/page095-img037.jpeg", width: 60%)

_Figure 17.1: Equipment_

_Placeholder for final art._
#pagebreak()

Your hero is going to need gear. A sword, some armor, a rope, a torch, a bedroll, and probably a ten-foot pole because someone at the table has read about pit traps. Equipment is the stuff between your hero and a bad day. Choose it well.

The tables in this chapter list weapons by required Disciplines, armor by weight class, cost, and slots, and adventuring gear by utility. Prices are in gold pieces (gp), the standard currency of the realms. A laborer earns about 1 gp a month. Prices vary by region and availability; the DA sets the cost in their world. Keep that in mind when you're haggling with the blacksmith. You're not just buying gear, you're spending someone's annual salary.

#pagebreak()

== Kits

A kit is how you are outfitted: the arms, the tools, and the habits that say what you do and where you came from. Your class says what you are. Your Disciplines say what you trained. Your cards carry the numbers. Your kit says what you brought.

A kit never adds a number. It grants no DR, no HP, no damage, and no bonus to any roll. What a kit grants is permission. It says which cards you can use, and it decides whether an attempt is fair or a long shot. If you need to know how hard you hit, look at your cards. If you need to know whether you can even try, look at your kit.

=== The Four Lines

Every kit is built from four lines: Armament, Covering, Focus, and Calling. Each option on a line has a price in kit points.

#figure(
  align(center)[#table(
    columns: (18.00%, 52.00%, 30.00%),
    align: (auto, auto, auto,),
    table.header([Line], [Options], [Points],),
    [*Armament*], [Unarmed], [0],
    [], [One-handed weapon], [1],
    [], [Ranged weapon], [1],
    [], [One-handed weapon and shield], [2],
    [], [Two-handed weapon], [2],
    [*Covering*], [None], [0],
    [], [Light armour], [1],
    [], [Medium armour], [2],
    [], [Heavy armour], [3],
    [*Focus*], [None], [0],
    [], [Holy, Arcane or Primal focus], [3],
    [*Calling*], [Any one vocation], [1],
  )],
  kind: table,
  outlined: false,
  numbering: none,
)

You take exactly one option from each of the four lines, and the four together are your primary kit. Your calling is what you were before you started adventuring, and it is the only line you must take. Its point is counted in every row below.

=== The Budget

You have six points to spend on your primary kit. Spend them well, because the leftovers have work to do.

#figure(
  align(center)[#table(
    columns: (34.00%, 22.00%, 44.00%),
    align: (auto, auto, auto,),
    table.header([A hero who...], [Spends], [Has left for packs],),
    [Wears no armour and carries a staff], [3], [3],
    [Wears no armour with a focus], [4], [2],
    [Wears light armour and a one-handed weapon], [3], [3],
    [Wears medium armour and a shield], [5], [1],
    [Wears heavy armour and a shield], [6], [0],
    [Wears heavy armour, a shield and a focus], [9], [impossible],
  )],
  kind: table,
  outlined: false,
  numbering: none,
)

A knight in plate with a shield has spent all six points on being hard to kill and carries nothing else. A light skirmisher with a one-handed weapon has three left, and three packs buys a great deal of capability the knight will never have. Heavy armor does not cost power, it costs kit. There is no best kit, because no kit is a superset of another at the same or lower cost. No build hands you everything, and every hero gives up something.

=== Packs

Leftover points buy packs, one point each. A pack is a capability, not a shopping list. Carrying the pack is what having the capability means.

Every hero has the Adventurer's Pack, and it costs nothing.

The free pack is comfort, not capability. It carries no rope, no pitons, no picks, and no charts, because "we forgot the rope" needs to stay possible.

A favour is not something you carry, but it is something you bring to a problem, and it works like every other pack.

=== Granted Kits

A kit point can also arrive as a grant: from a class, a talent, an ancestry gift, a faction, a favour earned in play, or taken off someone who no longer needs it. The thief's picks come off the thief, the scribe's case comes out of the wizard's study, the spade comes off the man in the grave. Treasure stops being coin and becomes capability: you wear what you took off the people who lost.

A talent that grants kit grants exactly one kit point. That point is the talent's entire payload, one point, nothing else. If the talent names a pack, the point is already spent. You are not choosing; the fiction chose. A talent that says you were a locksmith gives you the Thieves' Pack, not a free point to spend elsewhere.

That limit is the whole point. Without it, a hero could buy past the budget with talents, and a budget that can be exceeded is not a budget.

A class grants its signature pack at level 1. This is how the class's starting kit fits inside six points: the armor, weapon, and focus come out of the budget, and the tools of the trade arrive as the class's grant. See the class table below.

=== Re-Kitting at a Town

You may re-outfit at a town, and never in the field. Between towns you carry exactly what you brought and you deal with it. At a town, the whole kit is re-specified: armor, weapon, focus, and packs together, from what you carry plus whatever the local market offers.

This is what makes the kit a plan rather than a footnote. Going into the sewers you bring the climbing gear and the picks. Going to court you bring the papers and the disguise. Going into the barrow you bring the spade and the lantern oil. You choose against the job in front of you, and then you live with the choice.

=== Class Recommendations

No class is locked to a kit, and a hybrid is often the point. But if you want the classic shape of your class, start here.

The typical kit is a starting point, not a rule. Nothing stops a Protector from taking a focus and no armor, and a hybrid is often the interesting character. The table exists because "what would a Blade carry?" is a real question and a blank page is a bad answer.

== Weapons

A weapon is a promise your hero makes about who they are. The longsword on the hip, the twin daggers, the greataxe that will not fit through doorways, each one says something about the person carrying it. What a weapon does not do is decide how hard you hit. Discipline is permission: the Disciplines you have trained grant the attack ability cards you can take. Equipment is possession: the weapon in your hand is just the thing that happens to be there. Cards are damage: your attack ability cards carry the Weak, Standard, and Strong values (see @sec-chapter-talents-abilities), and the 3d6 attack roll decides which one you land. No separate damage dice.

Pick the weapon that fits your hero, not the one that looks best on paper. They all hit the same; you are the one doing the hitting.

#callout(type: "note", title: "Kit Gear", body: [
Your class starting kit assumes training with its gear: you can wield kit weapons and use kit armor and shields regardless of Discipline prerequisites. Attack ability cards still require their listed Disciplines, wielding a kit weapon does not grant the maneuvers that require them.
])

#callout(type: "note", title: "Melee Damage", body: [
Melee attacks add your Brawn to the damage row on your attack ability card; Finesse weapons use Agility instead. Missile and thrown attacks are flat, no attribute added. See @sec-chapter-talents-abilities for the cards and @sec-chapter-combat for the basic attack. The weapon never changes these numbers.

Improvised weapons (a crowbar swung as a club, a hammer in a pinch) deal 1/1/2 + Brawn, the Basic Unarmed floor. A thrown improvised object counts as a thrown attack: 1/2/3 flat, no attribute.
])

#callout(type: "note", title: "Discipline Combinations, Name Your Style", body: [
Weapons don't just require more of the same Discipline, they require specific combinations. A Longsword needs _2 Blades_. A Greatsword needs _2 Blades + 1 Heavy Weapon_. Your Discipline choices describe the kind of fighter you are, and that description decides which attack ability cards you can reach. A hero with a Greatsword is a different person than a hero with a Dagger, not a bigger number. Name the style you want, then pick the combination that says it out loud. The cards you can reach are the fighting style you have chosen.

*Heavy Weapon* Discipline represents training with large, two-handed weapons that rely on momentum and raw force rather than finesse. It opens the heaviest attack cards.
])

*Properties:*

- *Versatile*, can be wielded two-handed (Longsword only)
- *Finesse*, use Agility instead of Brawn for attack and damage (Dagger, Shortsword, Throwing Dagger)
- *Reach*, can attack targets 10 ft away (Spear, Halberd)
- *Thrown*, can be thrown (range 20/60 ft: Dagger, Handaxe, Spear, Throwing Dagger)
- *Light*, can be used as an off-hand weapon for two-weapon fighting (Dagger, Shortsword, Handaxe)
- *Loading*, requires a Maneuver to reload between shots (Crossbow only)
- *Two-Handed*, must be held in both hands and takes 2 slots (Spear, Halberd, Shortbow, Longbow, Crossbow). Compare *Versatile*, which *may* be used two-handed)

== Armor

Armor is what you wear: it is a choice about weight, cost, slots and donning time. Your Damage Reduction comes from your talents and abilities, not from your armor. See @sec-chapter-armor-shields

Shields: *Buckler* (1 Protection), *Shield* (1 Protection), *Tower Shield* (2 Protection, provides half cover). A shield enables Parry and Shield Block. Prices: see @sec-chapter-armor-shields

== Encumbrance

You're carrying your life. The question is how much of it fits on your back before the pack starts digging into your shoulders.

Slot-based system. You have 10 + (Brawn x 5) slots, with a floor of 5. Even a Brawn −2 hero carries the basics. Most items take 1 slot. Armor takes 2-4 slots. Two-handed weapons take 2 slots.

*One container at a time is exempt.* Only a single container keeps its contents off your sheet, and containers cannot be nested inside one another. A second sack or backpack carries gear like anything else: what's inside it counts against your slots. Choose which container is your working one, and pack accordingly.

A hero with Brawn +1 has 15 slots. A longsword (1 slot), a backpack (2 slots), a bedroll (2), a waterskin (1), torches (1), a quiver (1), and a dagger (1) is 9 slots. The remaining 6 slots cover the oddities, the spare rope, the lantern, the thing you picked up in the cellar that might be worth something.

== Adventuring Gear

The general store doesn't sell magic swords. It sells rope, rations, and the thousand small items that separate a prepared adventurer from a corpse. Here's what's on the shelf.

*Coins and Encumbrance:* 100 coins of any denomination take 1 slot. A pouch holds up to 50 coins slot-free. A sack holds up to 300 coins before it tears. After your first dragon hoard, invest in a wagon.

#callout(type: "note", title: "Starting Gear", body: [
New heroes take their class's starting kit (see @sec-chapter-classes); the DA may grant extra coin at campaign start.
])

== Mounts & Vehicles

A good horse is the difference between arriving fed and rested and arriving half-dead with blisters. A wagon is the difference between carrying out treasure and leaving it behind for the next batch of idiots. Pay attention.

=== Mounts

Mounts use a simplified stat block, HP, Speed, carrying capacity, and any special traits. They don't roll attacks (you do, from the saddle), but they can be targeted in combat. A dead horse is a tragedy. A dead horse in the middle of a chase is a catastrophe.

*Mount gear:* Saddle (10 gp), saddlebags (4 gp, hold 50 lbs), bit and bridle (2 gp), barding (light: 50 gp, +1 DR to mount; heavy: 200 gp, +3 DR to mount, Speed reduced by 10 ft). Barded mounts remain valid targets of focused fire; sustained attacks bring even an armored warhorse down. Feed costs 5 cp per day per mount. Stabling at an inn costs 5 sp per night.

#callout(type: "note", title: "Naming Your Mount", body: [
Give the horse a name. It'll die in session three and you'll all be genuinely upset. This is correct. This is the game working as intended.
])

=== Mounted Combat

Fighting from horseback isn't just "combat but taller." It changes the geometry of the fight. Use it.

*Charge Attack:* Here's the big one. When you move at least 20 feet in a straight line before making a melee attack from a mount, your attack deals +1 damage tier, the row one step up on the damage budget (see @sec-damage-budget). Strong is already the top row, so a Strong charge stays Strong.

#figure(
  align(center)[#table(
    columns: (50.00%, 50.00%),
    align: (auto, auto,),
    table.header([Normal Result], [Charge Result],),
    [Weak], [Standard],
    [Standard], [Strong],
    [Strong], [Strong],
  )],
  kind: table,
  outlined: false,
  numbering: none,
)

The charge must be in a straight line, no zigzagging through trees. The mount must have a clear path. The target must be within reach at the end of the movement. The mount can continue moving after the attack if it has movement remaining. Only one charge benefit per attack, so the off-hand strike of a two-weapon fight does not also claim it. A warhorse at full gallop with a lance is the closest thing to a thunderbolt you'll ever ride.

*Controlling a Mount:* Steering is free. A trained mount (a warhorse, or a riding horse with a rider who has Survival or Nature) follows the fiction, no roll required. To make the mount do something extra beyond its normal movement, spend the Command maneuver (see @sec-chapter-combat): the mount takes an extra move. In chaotic situations (explosions, dragon fear, the horse just took an arrow), the DA may call for a Survival or Nature check (Standard) to keep control.

*Fighting from a Moving Mount:* Ranged attacks made from a moving mount suffer a Bane. The horse's gait throws off your aim. If you have Survival or Nature at Adept or higher, the gait is nothing to you and the Bane is dropped. At Master rank, you ignore it entirely, you could thread an arrow through a keyhole at full gallop.

*Mount Death:* When your mount drops to 0 HP, it collapses. You're coming off. Make an Agility check (Standard 9-14) or take 3 damage and land Prone. On a Strong result, you leap clear and land on your feet, no damage, no Prone, all style.

*Dismounting:* Costs half your movement in normal circumstances. Emergency dismount (throwing yourself clear) is a free action but requires the same Agility check as mount death, you're choosing to take the risk before the horse goes down.

*Mounted vs. Foot:* Attacks against a mounted target from the ground carry a Bane, you're reaching up. Attacks from a mounted target against someone on foot carry a Boon, gravity is on your side. Neither applies when both combatants are mounted or both are on foot.

#callout(type: "tip", title: "The Cavalry Arrives", body: [
A party of four on horseback charging a line of goblins is one of the great joys of this game. The charge is the reason the section exists. Encourage your players to use terrain, momentum, and positioning. A mounted combatant who stands still might as well be on foot.
])

=== Vehicles

Sometimes you need to move more than yourself. Trade goods, siege equipment, the dragon's hoard you just liberated. Vehicles get it done.

#figure(
  align(center)[#table(
    columns: (17.31%, 11.54%, 9.62%, 13.46%, 11.54%, 23.08%, 13.46%),
    align: (auto, auto, auto, auto, auto, auto, auto,),
    table.header([Vehicle], [Cost], [HP], [Speed], [Crew], [Passengers], [Cargo],),
    [*Cart*], [50 gp], [30], [40 ft (draft horse)], [1], [3], [500 lbs],
    [*Wagon*], [100 gp], [50], [40 ft (draft horse)], [1], [6], [2,000 lbs],
    [*Carriage*], [300 gp], [40], [20 ft (draft horse, -2)], [1], [4], [200 lbs],
    [*Chariot*], [150 gp], [35], [45 ft (draft horse)], [1], [1], [100 lbs],
    [*Small Boat*], [200 gp], [40], [30 ft (oars), 45 ft (sail)], [2], [4], [500 lbs],
    [*River Barge*], [800 gp], [80], [20 ft (oars), 35 ft (sail)], [4], [10], [5 tons],
    [*Coastal Ship*], [5,000 gp], [200], [30 ft (sail)], [10], [30], [10 tons],
    [*Warship*], [10,000 gp], [300], [40 ft (sail + oars)], [40], [60], [5 tons],
  )],
  kind: table,
  outlined: false,
  numbering: none,
)

*Vehicle Rules:*

- *Speed:* The Speed column lists the vehicle's movement, with the draft animal's contribution in parentheses. A carriage and a chariot are heavier and less maneuverable, so their draft horse effectively moves at 20 ft. Exceeding cargo capacity halves Speed. Doubling it stops the vehicle entirely, the axle's not made of magic. A boat under oars moves at its oared speed; a favorable sail moves it at its sailed speed.
- *Crew:* The listed number is the minimum required to operate the vehicle. Half crew means Speed is halved. No crew means the vehicle drifts (water) or stops (land).
- *Vehicle HP:* When a vehicle reaches 0 HP, it's destroyed, a cart collapses, a ship breaks apart. Repairs cost 10% of the vehicle's value per HP restored and require a craftsperson and 1 day per 5 HP.
- *Combat on Vehicles:* Characters on a moving vehicle use the vehicle's Speed for relative positioning but act on their own initiative. The DA may call for Agility checks (Standard) to keep footing during sharp turns, collisions, or rough terrain. Falling off a wagon is embarrassing. Falling off a ship in a storm is a death sentence. Know the difference.
- *Chariots* are built for war: anyone riding in one has half cover from the sides and rear, already included in the price above. A cart hauls more and carries more people; a chariot outruns it and protects you while you fight from it.

*Upgrades:* Vehicles can be reinforced (+10 HP, costs 25% of base price), armored (passengers have half cover, costs 50% of base price), or outfitted with weapon mounts (ballista platform on a ship, crossbow mount on a wagon). Weapon mounts require a crew member to operate, and the damage comes from the attack card used to fire them.

#callout(type: "tip", title: "Chases", body: [
For vehicle vs. vehicle chases, a wagon fleeing bandits on horseback, a ship outrunning pirates, only the pursuer rolls, and the quarry's speed is the difficulty. Each round the pursuer's driver makes one roll on the core 3d6 (@sec-chapter-core-resolution), applying the Speed difference as a Boon or a Bane: a Boon if the pursuer is faster, a Bane if the quarry is. A 10 ft edge is one step, 30 ft is two, 60 ft or more is three. A Standard or Strong result closes one band of distance; a Weak result opens one. Closing three bands means the pursuer catches them, opening three means the quarry escapes, and short of that the chase simply continues, a wheel hits a rock, a sail tears, a horse stumbles, and the DA narrates the near miss.
])

Gear is the quiet part of the story. Your players will remember the goblins, the gold, and the horse that died in session three. They will also remember the weight of the longsword and the relief of finding oil for the lantern. Buy it well. Lose it badly. That's the adventure.

```
